title: The Bat and the Queen of the Moths
intro: A queen leads her moths to the candles and stops to tease a bat about his friendship with the dark. Shawqi included the fable in his Shawqiyyat. His friend Shakib Arslan quoted it to show how lightly Shawqi could write when the story called for it. The narrator leaves the encounter with the flames untold and brings back the opening words when the injured queen passes the bat again.

1.sharh: The queen arrives in the second half of the line. We see the bat first, then the visitor whose rank will so colour their conversation.

2.sharh: Her swarm looks like a royal procession. Its destination is also the familiar one for moths, the candle flames that draw them.

3.sharh: She has time on her way to the candles to turn aside to the bat. The laugh comes before the first word of her teasing.

4.sharh: In her eyes there is something discreditable about loving the dark. She judges his attachment by how its object looks next to her own bright favourite.

translation: Describe this black friend of yours,
5.sharh: She asks for a description after supplying one of her own. Darkness, obscurity and the lack of finery all count against the bat’s friend in her eyes.

translation: He said, “About him you have asked
the most truthful of those who know him.
6.sharh: The bat claims the authority of a friend who spends his waking hours in the dark. He answers her mockery as a genuine request.

7.sharh: The bat begins with the quality he prizes in a friend, fidelity. The next few lines give examples of what he means by it.

translation: In his keeping there is safety.
What he knows he keeps secret.
8.sharh: The shelter of darkness becomes the protection a host owes a guest. What happens under cover of night is as safe as a confidence kept between friends.

translation: when a friend makes a slip.
9.sharh: In the dark a fault goes unseen. The bat takes this quite literally and imagines a friend who kindly looks past a mistake.

translation: and gives the one who longs a hearing.
10.sharh: In the quiet after dark a lover can speak freely. The bat imagines the night itself as someone willing to listen.

translation: he is the one I hold dear.”
11.sharh: The bat has given his reasons. He ends on the value this particular friend has for him.

12.sharh: It is the narrator who calls the queen foolish. Her new speech will show what she values in a friend.

13.sharh: She insults the night by likening it to a man once enslaved and putting a price on him. Her choice of example has an irony of its own, since he became a ruler.

translation: compare with my companion the prince,
resplendent, there for all to see?
14.sharh: The prince is the light that the moths are flying towards. Its brilliance makes an impression on everyone, which matters greatly to the queen.

translation: If he is counted among my acquaintances,
I stand taller and share in his honour.
15.sharh: Merely being known to know the prince elevates her. She has described his effect on her standing before giving a single example of his friendship.

translation: And if I am asked about him
and where I stand with him,
16.sharh: She relishes being asked how close she is to him. We wait another line to hear what she tells her listeners.

translation: and turn away full of admiration.”
17.sharh: Her audience is made up of her peers. The glow she takes away comes as much from having impressed them as from the prince himself.

18.sharh: The bat gives her the royal style she has claimed throughout. The ceremonious address makes his dismissal sharper.

19.sharh: The bat sees a second kind of self-deception in believing that a rebuke will cure hers. He has said what he can about the night.

20.sharh: He lets her take the road she chose, but gives its destination another name. The reader already knows where the moths are headed.

translation: and went on her way boasting.
21.sharh: She carries her mockery and her pride away with her. The warning has made no difference to her course.

translation: a stretch of time ran out,
22.sharh: The storyteller lingers over the passing of a little time and skips the encounter with the flames. Its outcome will be visible on her body.

translation: and past the bat she flew,
23.sharh: The opening words return exactly. Where we might expect her throng and its proud flight to follow, the next line shows what has become of her.

translation: with parts of her body gone,
24.sharh: There is no glorious escort on this flight. Her own damaged body tells the part of the story the narrator left out.

translation: He came to her, absorbed in her plight.
25.sharh: The laughter has changed hands. It was the queen who laughed at the first meeting, and it is her weeping that draws the bat’s laughter now.

26.sharh: The bat brings back his warning. The question runs on into a judgement about friendship that holds whatever becomes of the queen.

translation: that many a friend held in slavery
shows a bright face in friendship
27.sharh: The bat answers the queen in the language of colour she used against his friend. Brightness now belongs to the friendship a person offers.

translation: and would ransom you like a prince,
with his life and all he treasures,
28.sharh: The enslaved friend acts with a prince’s generosity. The Arabic brings life and valuables even closer together in the sounds of nafs and nafis.

translation: while many a companion resembles light
29.sharh: The bat grants everything the queen has said about the attraction of light. He goes on to ask what sort of friend can live behind that appearance.

30.sharh: The darkness has moved inside the dazzling companion. What matters is the quality of the affection each of the two friends can give.

translation: To come close to him is to perish.”
31.sharh: The bonds that seemed to promise friendship turn out to be traps. The queen flew close enough to the light to put that last word to the test.

1.2.1.head: مَليكَة
1.2.1.meaning: A queen, the feminine of malik. The flock of moths has a royal leader in the fable.

1.2.2.head: الفَراش
1.2.2.meaning: Moths or butterflies collectively. These fly by night towards candles.

2.1.2.head: الجُموع
2.1.2.meaning: Throngs, here the swarms flying with their queen.

3.2.1.head: اِستَضحَكَ
3.2.1.meaning: Began to laugh or was overcome with laughter.

4.1.1.head: أَزرى
4.1.1.meaning: Brought into disrepute or treated with contempt.

4.1.2.head: الغَرام
4.1.2.meaning: A love that takes hold and will not let go.

5.2.1.head: الخامِل
5.2.1.meaning: Obscure, unnoticed, of little standing in people’s eyes.

5.2.2.head: المُجَرَّد
5.2.2.meaning: Stripped bare, here of the trappings that might attract notice.

6.2.2.head: واصِف
6.2.2.meaning: Those who describe him. The final pronoun refers to the night.

7.1.3.meaning: True to a friend and faithful to one’s obligations.

8.1.1.head: جِوار
8.1.1.meaning: Protection extended to someone who seeks refuge.

9.1.1.head: طَرف
9.1.1.meaning: The eye or its gaze. The bat pictures the night overlooking a friend’s fault.

9.1.2.head: كَليل
9.1.2.meaning: Dull or weak, said here of eyesight.

9.2.2.meaning: Slipped or made a momentary mistake.

11.1.1-2.head: جُملَةُ المَقال
11.1.1-2.meaning: “The sum of the words”, the conclusion of what has just been said.

13.1.2-4.head: أَبو المِسكِ الخَصِيّ
13.1.2-4.meaning: Abu al-Misk, the epithet of Kafur al-Ikhshidi, a Black eunuch who rose from slavery to rule Egypt in the tenth century CE. The queen alludes to his enslaved past.

13.2.3.head: المُستَرخَص
13.2.3.meaning: Valued cheaply by the person setting the price.

15.1.2.head: عَدَّ
15.1.2.meaning: Was counted among them. The verb is passive.

15.2.1.head: سَما
15.2.1.meaning: I rise in standing or distinction.

16.2.2.head: مَكان
16.2.2.meaning: Standing or favour, the place she holds in the prince’s regard.

17.1.1.head: فاخَرَ
17.1.1.meaning: Boast in competition with someone, claiming the greater distinction.

18.2.2.head: الأَريكَة
18.2.2.meaning: A furnished couch, traditionally one set under a canopy. Here it evokes a queen’s throne.

20.1.1-2.head: أَعطِني قَفاكِ
20.1.1-2.meaning: “Give me the back of your neck”, turn away from me and go.

21.2.2.head: مُفاخِر
21.2.2.meaning: Boasting of her friend and of the standing she claims through him.

22.1.2.head: ساعَة
22.1.2.meaning: A while or a short span of time.

24.2.3.head: الفَناء
24.2.3.meaning: Perishing or passing out of existence.

25.1.2.head: مُنهَمِك
25.1.2.meaning: Intent on something, wholly taken up with it.

25.2.3.meaning: Weeping. The usual buka' loses its final glottal stop here and rhymes with the preceding half.

27.2.1-3.head: أَبيَضُ وَجهِ الوُدّ
27.2.1-3.meaning: “Bright of face in friendship”, sincere in one’s affection. The image answers the queen’s taunt about colour.

28.1.1.head: فَدى
28.1.1.meaning: Would give up his own life or property to ransom you.

28.2.2.head: النَّفيس
28.2.2.meaning: Anything prized or precious. Its sound echoes nafs, one’s own life.

30.1.1.head: مُعتَكِر
30.1.1.meaning: Dark or murky, as a night that has grown very dark. The gloom here lies in the heart.

31.1.1.head: حَبل
31.1.1.meaning: Ropes or cords, such as a hunter uses to set snares. The reciter says jibaluhu, “his mountains”. Shawqi’s text reads hibaluhu, “his ropes”.

31.1.2.head: شَرَك
31.1.2.meaning: Snares or traps in which prey is caught.
